newsitem.title: CHINA: China not to import sugar in 1997, prices seen low.
newsitem.headline: China not to import sugar in 1997, prices seen low.

text.p: China is unlikely to import sugar this year because of sufficient domestic supply as well as imports already agreed from Cuba and recent high levels of smuggling, the China Daily Business Weekly said on Sunday.

"Supply and consumption of sugar in the domestic market will be balanced this year, and the country has no plan to import sugar through trade," it quoted Deng Chengshan, a division director of the State Planning Commission, as saying.
He did not rule out some imports through barter trade.
Output for the 1996/97 year was expected to reach 6.6 million tonnes, while consumption was estimated at 7.5 million tonnes, he said.
Imports of Cuban sugar through bilateral agreements, coupled with domestic reserves and the entry of large amounts of smuggled production from 1995 to early 1996 would fill the gap, he said.
Current prices in China are about 4,000 yuan ($480) per tonne, which is lower than the 4,550 yuan state-set price.
To maintain a balance between supply and demand, the government planned to control imports, stabilise sugar cane prices and establish a short-term reserve as well as a long-term one, he said.
Output hit 7.9 million tonnes in 1991/92 and this was followed by a price war among mills that also harmed farmers, he said.
Production plunged to 5.4 million tonnes in 1994/95 and prices surged to 4,800 yuan per tonne, opening the door to smuggling.
